consensus_summary: Sanctify means to set apart as holy for God; sanctification is primarily the process (or accomplished state) by which believers are made holy, separated from sin, and progressively conformed to Christ by the Spirit, with definitive, entire, theosis/sacramental, and cultic senses as alternatives.
book_summary: To cause, appoint, or acknowledge as holy by removing from common status, placing under an owner's claim for an appointed purpose, and treating or preparing it accordingly; God claims and fits for His use, people sanctify God/Name by treating Him as holy; moral cleansing and obedience fit the calling but are not the entire meaning.
consensus_core_identification: set apart / make holy for God (primary emphasis on progressive moral-spiritual transformation of believers)
book_core_identification: cause/appoint/acknowledge as holy via removal from common status under owner's claim for purpose plus corresponding treatment (moral fitting but not entire)
boundary_disagreement: Book centers ownership-claim, reverse sanctification of God/Name, and pure consecration of persons/objects (including cases without progressive moral change) as core; treats progressive inward renewal as non-entire. Consensus primary centers progressive moral transformation of believers and lists cultic/reverse/definitive as alternatives.
material_contradiction: None; both affirm setting apart as holy. Book subordinates rather than denies moral cleansing.
rationale: Minimum cores share the set-apart-as-holy referent. Book preserves that category but materially broadens and re-prioritizes: it elevates claim/purpose/treatment (including reverse and non-moral cases) to the definitional center while explicitly demoting the progressive moral process that forms the consensus primary meaning to a secondary fitting aspect. This is boundary and precision disagreement, not replacement of the central referent.
strongest_objection: The dominant Christian and NT usage for believers equates sanctification with progressive Spirit-wrought moral renewal (the view the book itself flags as 'commonly taught'), which the entry subordinates as incomplete.
